questions.q: What's the fundamental difference between a tiled and a floating dashboard object?
options: Tiled objects live in an automatically-adjusting grid; floating objects sit at a fixed position/size on top of that grid, unaffected by it
Tiled objects can only be worksheets; floating objects can only be images
Floating objects automatically resize when the browser window changes; tiled objects never do
There is no real difference — they're two names for the same behavior
questions.explain: Tiled objects claim a slot in a grid that reflows as objects are added, moved, or resized. Floating objects sit at an exact position/size and ignore the grid entirely.

questions.q: What does a Horizontal layout container do?
options: Arranges its child objects side by side, left to right, resizing them proportionally together
Stacks its child objects top to bottom
Converts all its children to floating objects automatically
Deletes any object placed inside it that isn't a worksheet
questions.explain: A Horizontal container arranges children left to right — resize the container and its children resize proportionally together, which is how predictable multi-column rows get built.

questions.q: Why do experienced Tableau developers typically build a dashboard skeleton out of nested Horizontal/Vertical containers rather than floating objects?
options: Because containers keep the layout predictable and responsive, while an all-floating dashboard can look fine on one screen and break on another since nothing reflows
Because Tableau doesn't allow more than two floating objects per dashboard
Because floating objects can't contain worksheets, only text
Because containers are required before any filter action can be added
questions.explain: Containers keep layout internally consistent as things are added or resized. An all-floating layout can look fine to the person who built it and break for anyone viewing it differently, since nothing automatically reflows.

questions.q: According to this lesson, which is a legitimate, targeted use of a floating object?
options: A KPI header banner or filter panel that deliberately needs to sit on top of another object, like something a Show/Hide button toggles
Every worksheet in the dashboard, so nothing ever moves
Only text boxes — worksheets should never be set to floating
Floating should never be used under any circumstances
questions.explain: Floating is meant for objects that deliberately need to overlap something else — a KPI banner over a chart, or a filter panel a Show/Hide button reveals — not as the default layout mode for an entire dashboard.

questions.q: Where do you set whether a newly-added object will be tiled or floating?
options: The Tiled/Floating toggle at the bottom of the Objects panel, set before dragging the object in
It can only be changed by deleting and rebuilding the entire dashboard
In the workbook's overall Preferences menu, which applies to every dashboard at once
Tiled and floating are fixed per object type and can never be changed
questions.explain: The Objects panel has a Tiled/Floating toggle — set it before dragging a new object in, since changing an existing object's mode afterward requires selecting it individually and toggling its own setting.
